title: Ocean voyage
sceneDesc: A schematic world map. The ship carrying the container follows the route from the port of loading to the port of discharge, through a canal and, on the transshipment route, via a hub.

1.yes: We're off! A small [[feeder]] ship takes me from {pol} towards the [[hub]] in {hub}.

2.yes: Feeder {feeder} sails to {hub}; the mainline connection on {vessel} is planned in the booking. [TO VERIFY:v54]
2.*: {vessel} {voyage} departs {pol}; port rotation and routing per the service schedule: {transit}. [TO VERIFY:v10]

narration.3: Schedule reliability matters: delays cascade into missed connections, berth windows and customer deadlines. ETAs are updated to customers through the voyage.

narration.1: In {hub}, I'm lifted off the feeder, wait a little in the yard, then I'm loaded onto the big ship {vessel} to Europe. That's [[transshipment]].
narration.2: [[transshipment|Transshipment]] at {hub}: discharge from the feeder, short dwell in the hub yard, reload onto {vessel}. Hub dwell is typically 1–3 days. [TO VERIFY:v73]
narration.3: Connection risk: feeder delays, hub congestion or mainline omissions roll boxes to the next mainline sailing. Transshipment boxes are re-planned at the hub. [TO VERIFY:v73]

1.GYE-ANR: We pass through the Panama Canal, a shortcut between the Pacific and the Atlantic.
1.*: We reach the Suez Canal, the shortcut between Asia and Europe — when it's safe to use.

2.GYE-ANR: Panama Canal transit: draft limits and water levels can restrict sizes and slots. [TO VERIFY:v55]
2.*: Suez routing saves 10+ days versus the Cape of Good Hope; since 2024 many services have been rerouted via the Cape for security reasons. [TO VERIFY:v63]

3.GYE-ANR: Canal restrictions translate into fewer slots or weight limits; carriers may levy surcharges. [TO VERIFY:v55]
3.*: Routing changes add transit time, fuel cost (BAF / contingency surcharges) and ripple effects on equipment and schedules. [TO VERIFY:v63] [TO VERIFY:v35]

1.reefer: Out at sea, my cooling unit keeps {cargo} at {setPoint}. The carrier watches my temperature from far away.
1.*: Out at sea, the crew check the lashings and the ship's route avoids the worst weather.

2.reefer: Reefer monitored by the crew and, often, remotely by the carrier's reefer team: set point, supply/return air, alarms. [TO VERIFY:v57]
2.tank: DG on board: the master holds the DG manifest and emergency information for each class and UN number. [TO VERIFY:v59]
2.*: The carrier tracks position and ETA; customer service updates customers if the ETA changes.

narration.3: Weather routing, lashing checks, reefer and DG monitoring. Incidents at sea (fire, stack collapse) can trigger [[general-average]]. [TO VERIFY:v76]

narration.1: Land ahoy! We're approaching {pod}. The carrier has already told the customer I'm coming.
narration.2: Approaching {pod}. The carrier has sent the [[arrival-notice]] and filed arrival data with {importCustoms}. [TO VERIFY:v66]
narration.3: Arrival: berth window confirmed, discharge list and import manifest transmitted; customs risk analysis already ran on the ENS. [TO VERIFY:v23] [TO VERIFY:v67]

3.yes: The feeder arrives late in {hub}: your box missed {vessel}. The next mainline sailing is in 7 days. The consignee has a DAP delivery deadline.
3.*: A fire breaks out in a cargo hold. It is extinguished, and the owners declare general average. Your customer's cargo was not damaged.

yes.1: Singapore is the world's largest transshipment hub: tens of millions of containers change ships there every year. [TO VERIFY:v73]
yes.2: Singapore handles about 39–41 million TEU a year, most of it transshipment. [TO VERIFY:v73]

*.1: Out of hundreds of millions of container moves each year, only a few hundred to a few thousand boxes are lost at sea. [TO VERIFY:v77]
*.2: The World Shipping Council reported 221 containers lost at sea in 2023 — a tiny fraction of the boxes shipped. [TO VERIFY:v77]

body.1: At the hub, my feeder ship meets the big mainline ship. I change ships there — no truck, no customs.
body.2: Transshipment boxes stay under the carrier's control; they're planned on the connecting vessel by the hub planners. Missed connections are the main risk. [TO VERIFY:v73]

GYE-ANR.1: The Panama Canal links the Pacific and the Atlantic, saving thousands of kilometres around South America.
GYE-ANR.2: Draft and water-level restrictions can limit vessel size and the number of daily transits; carriers adjust services and may add surcharges. [TO VERIFY:v55]

*.1: The Suez Canal saves a long trip around Africa. When it's not safe, ships take the Cape of Good Hope route instead — about 10 more days.
*.2: Since 2024, many Asia–Europe services have avoided the Red Sea and sailed via the Cape: longer transits, more fuel and new surcharges. Check the current situation. [TO VERIFY:v63]

body.2: The Cape of Good Hope route adds roughly 3,000–3,500 nautical miles and 10+ days versus Suez, depending on speed. [TO VERIFY:v63]

body.1: My cooling unit reports its temperature regularly, so the carrier can act if something goes wrong.
body.2: Remote reefer monitoring shows set point, supply/return air and alarms; deviations trigger crew intervention and customer information. [TO VERIFY:v57]
body.3: Temperature logs (unit download) are key evidence in claims; a set point error at booking can't be fixed at sea without the shipper's instruction. [TO VERIFY:v56]

body.1: Big waves make ships roll. Good lashing and correct weights keep containers safe.
body.2: Parametric rolling and heavy weather stress lashings; misdeclared weights increase the risk of stack collapse. [TO VERIFY:v77]

body.1: {transit}. The exact time depends on the route and the ports the ship calls at.
body.2: {transit}. Published transit times are port-to-port and indicative; door-to-door adds pre-carriage, dwell and on-carriage. [TO VERIFY:v10] [TO VERIFY:v54] [TO VERIFY:v55]

documents: **Manifest** — sent to destination customs and ports.
**Arrival notice** — prepared for the consignee and notify party. [TO VERIFY:v66]

documents.text: **Reefer temperature log** — downloaded on request or for claims. [TO VERIFY:v57]

costs: **BAF / emergency surcharges** when routing or fuel changes. [TO VERIFY:v35]

costs.text: **Transshipment** is included in the freight — no extra charge to the customer by default.

costs: **General average contributions** after major incidents. [TO VERIFY:v76]
risks: **Incidents at sea** → general average, delays, cargo loss. [TO VERIFY:v76]
jobs: **Network & vessel operations** — schedules, routing, port calls.
**Customer service** — ETA updates; **Claims** — incidents at sea.

incoNote.C: Under C-rules, the buyer carries the risk during the voyage although the seller paid the freight — insurance matters (CIF/CIP). [TO VERIFY:v18]
incoNote.F: Under F-rules, the buyer contracted this carriage and carries the voyage risk.
incoNote.E: Under EXW, the buyer carries the voyage risk.
incoNote.D: Under D-rules, the seller still carries the risk during the voyage.

1: The ocean voyage takes weeks; the route depends on canals and safety.
On some routes, the box changes ship at a hub: that's transshipment.
Reefers are monitored all the way; the customer is told before arrival.
2: Transit times are indicative and depend on routing (Suez, Cape, Panama). [TO VERIFY:v63]
Transshipment adds a hub dwell and a connection risk.
The arrival notice and import manifest are sent before arrival.
3: Missed connections: re-protect the box and update ETAs fast; check delivery commitments.
General average makes cargo owners provide security before delivery — insurance matters.
Routing changes drive surcharges and ripple through equipment and schedules.

1.prompt: The ship is approaching {pod}. What happens next?
1.hint: I'm still on the ship. How do I get onto the quay?

options.text: The ship berths and a crane unloads me onto the quay.
options.confirm: Yes! At {pod}, a quay crane discharges me and I go to the import yard.

options.text: A truck drives onto the ship to pick me up.
options.why: Container ships are worked by cranes, not trucks driving on board.
options.realLife: Only roll-on/roll-off ships carry trucks on board.
options.whenRight: On ro-ro ships (cars, trailers) — a different kind of shipping.

options.text: I'm delivered straight to the customer's door.
options.why: I have to be unloaded and cleared by customs first.
options.realLife: No box leaves the terminal without customs and carrier release.

options.text: Berthing and discharge; the box goes to the import yard while customs assesses the manifest data and the consignee prepares clearance.
options.confirm: Correct. Discharge follows the discharge list; customs has already risk-assessed the ENS and manifest. [TO VERIFY:v67]

options.text: The box is delivered directly from the ship's side to the consignee's truck.
options.why: Import boxes go to the yard; customs and carrier releases come first.
options.realLife: Direct delivery is exceptional and needs prior clearance.

options.text: Customs clears the goods automatically on discharge, without a declaration.
options.why: Goods need an import declaration (or another customs procedure) to enter free circulation.
options.realLife: Undeclared goods stay in temporary storage, then face penalties.
options.whenRight: Transit or transshipment procedures follow different rules.

options.text: The box is transshipped again at {pod} onto a feeder.
options.why: {pod} is the final port of discharge in this booking.
options.realLife: Extra transshipment would add time and cost not booked.
options.whenRight: When the booking's final port is a feeder port beyond the hub.

yes.prompt: Case: the box missed its mainline connection at {hub}; next sailing in 7 days; DAP delivery deadline at risk. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the customer the new ETA now and look for faster re-protection (another service or partner slot); document the cause.
options.confirm: Right. Re-protection options depend on network and slot agreements; transparent, early ETA updates let the seller (DAP) manage its buyer and costs. [TO VERIFY:v73]

options.text: Wait for the next mainline without informing anyone.
options.why: The customer loses the chance to adapt.
options.realLife: Contract penalties and a damaged relationship.

options.text: Ask the customer to pay a new freight for the next sailing.
options.why: The booked freight covers carriage to {pod}, including the connection.
options.realLife: Charging again would breach the contract of carriage.
options.whenRight: Only if the customer asks for a premium service.

options.text: Truck the box from {hub} to Europe.
options.why: There's no practical road link; it's not an option.

*.prompt: Case: fire in a hold, general average declared; your customer's cargo is undamaged. What must the consignee do to obtain delivery?

options.text: Provide general average security — usually a GA bond plus an insurer's guarantee — before the cargo is released.
options.confirm: Right. All cargo interests contribute to GA, even undamaged ones. Insured cargo: the insurer provides the guarantee; uninsured cargo may need a cash deposit. [TO VERIFY:v76]

options.text: Nothing — undamaged cargo is not affected.
options.why: GA is shared by all interests in proportion to value, damaged or not.
options.realLife: Release is withheld until security is provided.

options.text: Pay the full cost of the fire.
options.why: GA is shared proportionally among ship and all cargo.
options.realLife: Each interest pays its share after adjustment, which can take years.

options.why: The B/L doesn't change; security is what's required.
options.realLife: Release depends on GA security plus the usual release conditions.
